outline: All electromagnetic waves are transverse and travel at $c=3.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in free space. Their wavelength increases in the order gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Visible wavelengths are about 400–700 nm. In free space $c=f\lambda$ links wavelength and frequency: longer wavelength means lower frequency.

misconceptions.statement: Different electromagnetic regions travel at different speeds in free space.
misconceptions.refutation: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed c in free space.
misconceptions.contrast: Wavelength and frequency differ, but their product is c.

misconceptions.statement: Microwaves with centimetre wavelengths are radio waves.
misconceptions.refutation: The approximate microwave range is 1 mm to 30 cm; radio wavelengths are roughly 30 cm to 100 km.
Visible light spans approximately 400–700 nm in free space.
misconceptions.contrast: 500 nm is visible; 300 nm is ultraviolet.

misconceptions.statement: Increasing wavelength also means increasing frequency.
misconceptions.refutation: In free space c=fλ, so frequency falls as wavelength rises.
misconceptions.contrast: Gamma rays have shortest wavelengths and highest frequencies.

flashcards.back: All electromagnetic waves are transverse waves and travel with the same speed $c=3.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in free space.

9702-7.4.1.motivate: A microwave pulse and a flash of visible light cross the same distance in free space. Which arrives first?
9702-7.4.1.establish: All electromagnetic waves are transverse waves: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel. In free space every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed, $c=3.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Radio, microwave, visible and gamma radiation all share this speed. Their frequencies and wavelengths differ, but $c=f\lambda$ stays the same in free space. A longer wavelength therefore pairs with a lower frequency, not a lower speed.
9702-7.4.1.connect: This extends the transverse-wave idea from 7.2. It also lets you convert frequencies to wavelengths before identifying an electromagnetic region.
9702-7.4.1.note:
- All electromagnetic waves are transverse.
- All travel at the same speed $c$ in free space.
- In free space $c=f\lambda$.
9702-7.4.1.self_explain: Why can two electromagnetic waves have different frequencies yet the same speed in free space?

9702-7.4.2.motivate: A telescope detects a 2 cm wave. Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum is it?
9702-7.4.2.establish: Recall the principal regions in order of increasing wavelength in free space: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves and radio waves. Approximate ranges are gamma rays below $10^{-11}$ m, X-rays about $10^{-11}$ to $10^{-8}$ m, ultraviolet about $10^{-8}$ to $4\times10^{-7}$ m, visible light 400–700 nm, infrared from 700 nm to 1 mm, microwaves from 1 mm to 30 cm, and radio waves from 30 cm to about 100 km. The limits are approximate. Frequency goes in the opposite order because $c=f\lambda$.
9702-7.4.2.connect: Use these ranges after converting prefixes: 2 cm is 0.02 m and therefore lies in the microwave range.
9702-7.4.2.note:
- Increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio.
- Microwaves are roughly 1 mm–30 cm; radio waves begin around 30 cm.
- Increasing frequency reverses this order.
9702-7.4.2.self_explain: Why does the list of regions reverse when arranged by increasing frequency?

9702-7.4.3.motivate: A wavelength of 0.5 micrometres sounds tiny. Can the eye detect it?
9702-7.4.3.establish: Wavelengths of approximately 400–700 nm in free space are visible to the human eye. Since $1\ \mathrm{\mu m}=1000\ \mathrm{nm}$, the same interval is 0.4–0.7 micrometres. A 0.5 micrometre wave is 500 nm and is visible. Below about 400 nm is ultraviolet; above about 700 nm is infrared. Convert units before classifying a wave.
9702-7.4.3.connect: Visible light is the narrow band between ultraviolet and infrared in the wider electromagnetic spectrum.
9702-7.4.3.note:
- Visible light in free space spans about 400–700 nm.
- This equals 0.4–0.7 micrometres.
- 500 nm is visible; 300 nm is ultraviolet.
9702-7.4.3.self_explain: How do you decide whether a wavelength written in micrometres is visible?
